title: Microbiology MCQ Draft – Specimen Diagnostics, Resistance, IPC, and Immunology

questions.stem: When should a diagnostic specimen ideally be collected?
options: After a full course of empiric antimicrobials
questions.explanation: Collection before therapy maximizes recovery of viable pathogens.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which medium is recommended for transporting enteric pathogens in stool?
questions.explanation: Cary-Blair preserves enteric bacterial pathogens during transport.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which organism should not be refrigerated during transport because it is cold-sensitive?
questions.explanation: The source identifies Shigella as cold-sensitive and unsuitable for refrigeration without medium.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which transport system improves survival of fastidious organisms such as Neisseria and Haemophilus?
questions.explanation: Charcoal-containing systems neutralize toxic substances and improve survival.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the gold-standard urine specimen for an infant or unclear UTI case?
questions.explanation: Suprapubic aspirate bypasses urethral contamination and is the sterile gold standard.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What additive is used in grey-top urine tubes when transport is delayed beyond 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: Boric acid inhibits overgrowth while preserving urine culture characteristics.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: How should CSF suspected of containing Neisseria meningitidis or Haemophilus influenzae be handled?
options: Process immediately at room temperature and do not refrigerate
questions.explanation: Rapid processing at room temperature is required because these organisms are cold-sensitive.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What system is required for NAAT targeting Chlamydia trachomatis or Mycoplasma genitalium?
questions.explanation: NAAT systems use specialized liquid buffers that stabilize target nucleic acids.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which specimen is appropriate for suspected C. difficile testing?
options: Liquid or unformed stool in a clean container
questions.explanation: C. difficile testing requires liquid or unformed stool; swabs are unacceptable in the source.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is preferred for a deep wound infection or abscess?
options: Tissue biopsy or direct needle aspiration of pus
questions.explanation: Tissue and pus aspirates avoid surface colonizers and outperform superficial swabs.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Why should wound swabs for anaerobic culture not be refrigerated?
questions.explanation: Refrigeration is detrimental to anaerobic and other fastidious organisms.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which protocol best describes lower-respiratory sputum collection?
options: Rinse with water, deep-breathe, cough deep sputum into a sterile cup before antibiotics
questions.explanation: Deep bronchial sputum, at least 1 mL, should be collected before antibiotics while avoiding saliva.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which eye specimen requires immediate bedside inoculation into aerobic and anaerobic blood-culture bottles?
options: Vitreous aspirate or anterior-chamber fluid in endophthalmitis
questions.explanation: Tiny endophthalmitis samples require immediate inoculation or transport within 30 minutes.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Why are synthetic flocked swabs preferred over cotton swabs?
options: Cotton may contain inhibitory fatty acids and toxic substances
questions.explanation: Cotton residues can impair viability of fastidious bacteria.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which situation is a valid reason to reject a specimen?
options: Leaking container, wrong medium, insufficient volume, or major delay
questions.explanation: Leaking, inadequate, improperly transported, or delayed specimens require rejection.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What method enhances recovery of Yersinia enterocolitica from stool?
options: Alkaline peptone water at room temperature
questions.explanation: Yersinia benefits from prolonged cold enrichment at 4°C.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which details belong on a microbiology requisition?
options: Patient identifiers, location, date/time, history, provisional diagnosis, and clinician signature
questions.explanation: Complete clinical context and identifiers guide processing and interpretation.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is required when handling clinical specimens?
options: Universal precautions, barrier PPE, and leak-proof secondary bags
questions.explanation: Specimens are biohazards and require PPE and sealed double-pouch transport.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which agar is used to screen stool for E. coli O157:H7?
questions.explanation: E. coli O157:H7 fails to ferment sorbitol, supporting use of Sorbitol-MacConkey agar.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Why is specimen quality foundational to diagnostic microbiology?
options: Poor collection can cause false results and inappropriate therapy
questions.explanation: Poor specimen handling produces misleading results and can worsen outcomes.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which specimen best avoids contamination when investigating an abscess?
questions.explanation: Direct aspirate samples the infected focus rather than colonized surface flora.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: A delayed CSF sample for suspected meningococcal disease should be handled by which principle?
options: Keep at room temperature and process urgently
questions.explanation: Urgent room-temperature processing protects recovery of cold-sensitive pathogens.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which test format uses a liquid buffer to stabilize nucleic acid rather than preserve viable organisms?
questions.explanation: NAAT collection tubes stabilize target nucleic acids for molecular testing.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which stool consistency is acceptable for routine C. difficile testing in the source?
questions.explanation: The source specifies liquid or unformed stool and rejects swabs for this testing.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What does Sorbitol-MacConkey selection exploit for E. coli O157:H7?
questions.explanation: The organism fails to ferment sorbitol, enabling screening on this agar.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which collection error most directly risks a false-negative culture?
questions.explanation: Antimicrobials can reduce viable pathogen recovery.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which sample is least suitable for deep wound culture?
questions.explanation: Superficial swabs are more likely to recover colonizers than deep pathogens.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which pair is specifically described as fastidious and cold-sensitive in CSF?
questions.explanation: The source specifically warns that meningococcus and H. influenzae are cold-sensitive.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the minimum sputum volume stated for lower respiratory culture?
questions.explanation: The source specifies at least 1 mL of deep bronchial sputum.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the main diagnostic advantage of a complete clinical request form?
options: It provides context for processing, organism selection, and urgency
questions.explanation: Clinical context helps the laboratory choose appropriate processing and interpretation.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: How should a tiny vitreous sample for endophthalmitis be handled?
options: Immediately inoculate aerobic and anaerobic blood-culture bottles
questions.explanation: Immediate bedside inoculation maximizes recovery from the very small volume.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of charcoal in Amies/Stuart transport media?
options: To neutralize toxic substances and improve survival
questions.explanation: Charcoal neutralizes inhibitory substances affecting fastidious organisms.

clinicalReference.source: Diagnostic Microbiology & Specimen Collection (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the foundational property of an ideal antimicrobial?
questions.explanation: Selective toxicity harms the pathogen while minimizing host-cell injury.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What causes high-level methicillin resistance in MRSA?
questions.explanation: mecA encodes altered PBPs such as PBP2a with reduced beta-lactam binding.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which disk is the standard surrogate screen for MRSA?
questions.explanation: The cefoxitin disk is the reliable surrogate for mecA-mediated resistance.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What defines metallo-beta-lactamases such as NDM, VIM, and IMP?
options: Zinc-dependent hydrolysis of most beta-lactams except aztreonam
questions.explanation: MBLs require zinc and hydrolyze carbapenems and other beta-lactams except aztreonam.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which combination is described for MBL-producing gram-negative infections?
questions.explanation: Aztreonam escapes MBL hydrolysis while avibactam inhibits co-produced serine carbapenemases.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What does a clindamycin D-zone indicate?
questions.explanation: Erythromycin induces ribosomal methylation, flattening the clindamycin zone into a D.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is biofilm tolerance?
options: Temporary physiological survival of surface communities at high drug concentrations
questions.explanation: Biofilm tolerance is a reversible physiological state in an EPS matrix, distinct from genetic resistance.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: How can Pseudomonas aeruginosa lose OprD and resist imipenem?
questions.explanation: OprD loss reduces outer-membrane permeability and may combine with efflux.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which antimicrobial type is emphasized for endocarditis, meningitis, or neutropenic sepsis?
questions.explanation: The source identifies bactericidal therapy as required in these severe or sanctuary-site infections.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What does susceptibility category I mean in updated CLSI/EUCAST guidance?
questions.explanation: I indicates efficacy is expected with increased exposure through dosing or pharmacokinetic optimization.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What genetic element spreads blaNDM-1 rapidly between bacteria?
questions.explanation: Mobile plasmids facilitate horizontal transfer of blaNDM-1.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which platform provides rapid multiplex PCR from blood cultures in about one hour?
questions.explanation: These syndromic panels detect pathogens and resistance targets rapidly.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: When should empiric antimicrobials be reviewed for de-escalation?
questions.explanation: Review and de-escalation at 48–72 hours reduces toxicity and resistance pressure.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which practice is discouraged to avoid treating colonization?
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic Candida in urine should not be treated without clinical infection.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of chlorhexidine washes and nasal mupirocin before surgery?
options: Reduce MRSA carriage and surgical-site infection
questions.explanation: Preoperative decolonization targets skin and nasal MRSA carriage.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: About what proportion of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source states that roughly 70% originate from animal reservoirs.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which event fostered complacency that infectious diseases had been conquered?
questions.explanation: Smallpox eradication, alongside antibiotic discoveries, fostered a false sense of security.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which factor drives zoonotic spillover?
questions.explanation: Deforestation, urbanization, and agriculture increase contact with reservoirs.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which pathogen class has high mutation and recombination potential via drift and shift?
questions.explanation: RNA viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 evolve rapidly through mutation and reassortment.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is the natural reservoir and route for Lassa fever?
questions.explanation: Mastomys rodents shed virus in urine and droppings that contaminate food or environments.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which vector transmits Oropouche virus?
options: Culicoides paraensis midges and some mosquitoes
questions.explanation: The source identifies biting midges and certain mosquitoes.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is the primary reservoir host for MERS-CoV?
questions.explanation: Dromedary camels are identified as the primary reservoir and zoonotic source.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What describes the spread of mpox clades IIb and Ib?
options: From regional African outbreaks to global multi-country emergencies
questions.explanation: The source describes transition from geographically confined outbreaks to global dissemination.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which fungus is listed as critical-priority multidrug-resistant yeast?
questions.explanation: Candida auris is described as a critical-priority MDR yeast causing healthcare outbreaks.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What drives azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus?
questions.explanation: Environmental agricultural azole exposure can drive cross-resistance.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: How is Sporothrix brasiliensis commonly transmitted in South America?
options: Infected cat scratches, bites, and contact
questions.explanation: The source describes zoonotic transmission from infected cats.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is the core One Health philosophy?
options: Integration of human, animal, and environmental health
questions.explanation: One Health requires cross-sector collaboration because these domains are interconnected.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What do crowdsourced genomic surveillance and metagenomics enable?
options: Early identification and tracking of pathogen evolution
questions.explanation: They support early detection and monitoring of variants and genetic shifts.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What amplifies nosocomial transmission during Ebola or MERS outbreaks?
options: Overwhelmed facilities, PPE shortages, and poor IPC
questions.explanation: Weak IPC and PPE shortages turn healthcare facilities into transmission amplifiers.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What does a very high R0 indicate?
options: Easier spread and more difficult control
questions.explanation: A high basic reproductive number signals high transmissibility and harder containment.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: Which measures include masks, gowns, gloves, isolation, quarantine, and contact tracing?
questions.explanation: IPC includes standard and transmission-based precautions plus isolation and tracing.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What is the most sustainable approach to emerging and re-emerging infections?
options: Early detection, rapid response, surveillance, and strong public health infrastructure
questions.explanation: The source emphasizes proactive surveillance, rapid response, and strengthened systems.

clinicalReference.source: Antimicrobial Resistance (Lectre No. 2)

questions.stem: What defines an antigen or immunogen?
options: A substance that stimulates a specific immune response
questions.explanation: An antigen is a substance capable of stimulating a specific immune response.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What immunology milestone did Pasteur achieve in 1885?
options: First attenuated rabies vaccine in a human
questions.explanation: Pasteur administered an attenuated rabies vaccine to Joseph Meister.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which features distinguish adaptive from innate immunity?
questions.explanation: Adaptive immunity has specificity, diversity, and long-lasting memory.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Where do T lymphocytes mature and what immunity do they mediate?
questions.explanation: T cells mature in the thymus and mediate cell-mediated immunity.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: In serum electrophoresis, where are antibodies primarily found?
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulins migrate mainly with the gamma-globulin fraction.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the basic structure of a monomeric immunoglobulin?
options: Two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulfides
One secretory component and three light chains
questions.explanation: A monomer contains two identical heavy and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is most abundant in serum and crosses the placenta?
questions.explanation: IgG represents 75–85% of serum immunoglobulin and crosses the placenta.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What structure characterizes secretory IgA?
options: Dimer joined by J-chain and secretory component
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA is a protected J-chain-linked dimer in mucosal secretions.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin appears first in primary infection and strongly activates complement?
questions.explanation: IgM is mainly pentameric, appears early, and fixes complement.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which antibody mediates type I hypersensitivity and helminth defense?
questions.explanation: IgE binds mast cells and basophils and is associated with allergy and helminths.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is the primary recognized function of IgD?
questions.explanation: IgD is a membrane-bound B-cell receptor on B cells alongside IgM.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What characterizes a secondary immune response?
options: Short lag and massive IgG in primary response
Prompt, powerful, prolonged response with high IgG
questions.explanation: Memory produces a rapid, high-titer, predominantly IgG response on re-exposure.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: How is passive immunization achieved and what is its limitation?
options: Transfer of preformed antibodies; temporary protection
questions.explanation: Passive immunity supplies antibodies immediately but does not create lasting host memory.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: What is a major disadvantage of live-attenuated vaccines?
questions.explanation: Attenuated organisms carry a small risk of reverting toward virulence.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which group consists of killed/inactivated vaccines in the source?
options: DTPw, whole-cell typhoid, IPV, rabies, and hepatitis A
questions.explanation: The source lists these as killed vaccines that remain antigenic but often require multiple doses.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)

questions.stem: Which is NOT a valid contraindication to routine immunization?
options: Minor URI, mild diarrhea, low-grade fever, prematurity, or penicillin allergy
questions.explanation: Minor illness, prematurity, and penicillin allergy are not contraindications in the source.

clinicalReference.source: Immunology and Serology (Dr. Fatiem T. Gammoudi)
